title: The last things
for: I want to know what happens at the end
subtitle: Ten sessions on the Christian hope, from death and the waiting after it through Christ's return, the resurrection, judgment, hell and the new creation, to speaking of hope to someone who grieves.
intro: The church calls the doctrine of the last things eschatology, and it covers what happens at death, the return of Christ, the resurrection of the body, the final judgment and the destiny of the world. These ten sessions take it a piece at a time. Each asks you to say the doctrine in your own words, find where it comes from in Scripture, see why the church holds it, and explain it simply to someone else.

The creeds bind the return of Christ, the resurrection of the body, the judgment and the life everlasting, and those are confessed plainly here. The shape of the thousand years, the state of the dead before the resurrection and the nature of hell are questions on which faithful Christians differ, and each view is given in its own strongest voice. The author is a Baptist pastor, and Baptists have held more than one view on most of them.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a small group through The last things. The group suits Christians who want to understand what the church hopes for and why, and anyone from outside the faith who wants to hear that hope from the inside rather than from a chart or a novel. The leader's task is to keep the group in Scripture, to confess plainly what the creeds confess, and to give room where faithful churches differ.

This track touches death and grief in almost every session. Expect that someone in the group will be carrying a recent loss, a frightening diagnosis or fear about someone they love. Each person reads the session, opens its page and does what it asks before the group meets. The meeting talks over what people found, using the group guide for that session, which is gathered below in order.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to ten people is a good size. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, once a week or once a fortnight, for ten meetings, and keep the end time you promised. Say at the start that no one needs to read every word of the doctrine pages, only enough to bring one thing they noticed and one question. A leader doesn't need to be a theologian. A leader needs to have done the reading, to be willing to say that they don't know, and to care more about the people than the timeline.

sections.title: The room
body: A table works best, with Bibles open and paper for notes. Say at the first meeting that anyone may pass on any question, that the group will disagree about the millennium and perhaps about hell and that this is allowed, and that no one has to pray aloud. Keep a box of tissues on the table without remark. What people say about their own lives and losses stays in the room, unless someone is in danger.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Ten minutes: one person reads the verse aloud, and the passage around it, while the others follow.
Thirty-five minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order. Ask where each answer is found, in Scripture or on the page.
Ten minutes: each person states the session's doctrine in a sentence of their own, as if to a friend.
Five minutes: the prayer prompt, in the group's own words.
Five minutes: name the next session and the page it opens, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: First ask what order the question is. That Christ will return in person, that the dead will be raised, that he will judge the living and the dead, and that his kingdom will have no end are first-order; the creeds confess them and the sessions say so plainly. The millennium, the rapture, the state of the dead before the resurrection and the nature of hell are questions faithful Christians answer differently, and the group should leave them open.

Let each view be stated in a form its own defenders would accept before anyone argues against it. Questions about a particular person, a parent or child who has died, are not abstract. Answer them gently, say what Scripture says and no more, and leave the judgment where Abraham left it, with the Judge of all the earth.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: When the study touches someone's grief, stop and listen. Thank them for saying it, don't explain their loss for them, and don't hurry back to the outline. Never use the doctrine to tell someone how to feel, and never tell a grieving person what a loved one's death was for. Ask whether they would like the group to go on or to pause, and speak with them on their own afterwards.

If someone says that a partner, a leader or anyone else is harming them or a child, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret. A child who may be in danger is a matter for the authorities, not only for the group.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when what they carry has become too heavy to set down: grief that has taken their sleep or appetite for weeks, fear of death or of judgment that will not let them rest, a diagnosis they are facing alone, harm done to them, or any sign that they no longer want to be alive. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor, and the kindest thing is often to stay with the person while they make the first call.

sessions.title: Death
teaching: Christians don't call death natural. Many people today speak of it as a part of life to be accepted, and some of that is wise; Scripture also teaches us to number our days. But the Bible names death as an intruder, the shadow that fell over every human story in the garden, and Paul calls it “The last enemy to be destroyed” (1 Corinthians 15:26). That isn't morbid. It is the only view of death that lets grief be honest. If death is natural, mourning is a failure to accept reality. If death is an enemy, tears are the right response to a wrong, and Jesus wept at a grave he was about to empty.

Christians also refuse to treat death as the final word. Hebrews says the Son shared our flesh and blood so that by his death he might break the power of the one who holds the power of death, and free “those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death” (Hebrews 2:15). Late medieval Christians wrote handbooks on the art of dying well, and the church once taught its people to prepare for death as a matter of faith. Much of that habit has been lost, and many believers meet death unready. To face it honestly is not despair. It is the beginning of a hope that can survive a hospital room.

sessions.question: Do you think of death more as something natural to accept or as an enemy to be defeated, and how does that shape the way you grieve?
sessions.do: Read 1 Corinthians 15:20-28 and John 11:32-44. Write down what each says about death, and notice that Jesus weeps before he raises Lazarus.

verse.text: The last enemy to be destroyed is death.

care: If you are grieving someone who has died, these verses do not ask you to stop grieving. Jesus wept at his friend's grave (John 11:35). Paul says believers grieve, but not “like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: How was death talked about, or not talked about, in the home you grew up in?
discuss: How would you explain to a friend why Christians call death an enemy rather than a natural part of life?
What does it mean that Jesus wept at Lazarus's grave when he knew he was about to raise him?
What would it look like for a church to help its people prepare to die well?
group.pray: Pray for anyone in the group who is grieving, and for those you know who are facing death now.

sessions.title: Between death and the resurrection
teaching: The Christian hope is the resurrection of the body at Christ's return, which raises an honest question: what happens to those who die before then? The New Testament answers in a few short lines rather than a map. Jesus promised the dying thief, “today you will be with Me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43). Paul, weighing his own death, wrote of his desire “to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed” (Philippians 1:23). Theologians call this the intermediate state. Most of the church has read these texts as teaching that believers who die are with Christ at once, consciously and at rest, while the body waits. It is better than now. It is not yet the end.

The traditions describe the waiting differently. Most Protestants, with the Heidelberg Catechism and the Westminster Confession, teach conscious presence with Christ. Catholic teaching holds that those who die in God's grace but not yet fully purified pass through purgatory, a cleansing on the way to the vision of God, and that the living may pray for them. The Orthodox pray for the departed and speak of a foretaste of glory or of loss before the judgment, without the Western doctrine of purgatory. Some Christians, Seventh-day Adventists among them, hold that the dead sleep until the resurrection, taking Paul's language of sleep at its word. Every view confesses that the dead are held by God until the resurrection.

sessions.question: What comfort does it give you that the dead in Christ are with him now, and what comfort is still being saved for the resurrection?
sessions.do: Read 2 Corinthians 5:1-10 and Philippians 1:19-26. Write down what Paul longs for in each, and notice whether he longs more to be unclothed or to be clothed.

verse.text: We are confident, then, and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.

If your grief feels too heavy to carry, please tell someone you trust: a pastor, a friend or a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: The return of Christ
teaching: The Nicene Creed confesses that Christ will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, and that his kingdom will have no end. The angels at the ascension told the disciples that “This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11). The return is personal: the same Jesus, scars and all. It is public, not a secret or a spiritual mood. And it is the hinge of history, when the dead are raised and the world is set right. This is first-order. A Christianity without the return has no ending, only a sentiment.

The New Testament is just as firm that no one knows when. Jesus said, “No one knows about that day or hour” (Matthew 24:36), and church history is crowded with people who thought they did. The followers of William Miller waited through the night of October 22, 1844, and called the morning after the Great Disappointment. The cost of setting dates is always the same: faith tied to a calendar breaks when the calendar does. Scripture's alternative is readiness, not calculation. Servants keep their lamps lit and do their work, because the master may come at any hour. The early church prayed in Aramaic, Maranatha, come, Lord, and that prayer is still the right posture.

sessions.title: The resurrection of the body
teaching: The Apostles' Creed ends with the resurrection of the body, not the immortality of the soul, and the choice was deliberate. Greek philosophy, and the Gnostic teachers the early church resisted, pictured salvation as escape from the body. The Christian hope is the body raised and made new, as Christ's was. Paul ties the two together: “But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). Firstfruits are the first sheaf of a harvest that is surely coming. Easter is not only evidence that Jesus lives. It is the beginning of what will happen to everyone who belongs to him.

The resurrection body is the same person, and yet changed. Paul reaches for the picture of a seed: what is sown perishable is raised imperishable, sown in weakness, raised in power, sown a natural body, raised a spiritual body. A spiritual body does not mean a ghostly one. It means a body wholly given life by the Spirit. The risen Jesus ate fish and was touched, and still came through locked doors. The church has never claimed to know the mechanics. It confesses the promise: the body you were given matters, it will be raised, and it will be glorious. That changes how Christians treat the sick, the disabled, the old and the dead.

care: It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: The millennium
teaching: Revelation 20 speaks of a thousand years in which Satan is bound and the faithful reign with Christ. The track Where Christians differ set out the four main readings; here it is worth going a layer deeper, into why each has convinced careful readers. Historic premillennialists, with early writers like Irenaeus, read the chapter in sequence after Christ's return in chapter 19, and take the two resurrections of verses 4 and 5 as two real events. Amillennialists, following Augustine, note that Revelation is a book of symbols and repeated cycles, that its numbers are seldom arithmetic, and that the binding of Satan echoes Jesus' binding of the strong man in the Gospels. Postmillennialists read the promises that the knowledge of the Lord will fill the earth as reaching their fulfillment before the end.

Dispensational premillennialism, shaped by John Nelson Darby in the nineteenth century and spread by the Scofield Reference Bible of 1909, added a sharp distinction between Israel and the church and a rapture of believers before a seven-year tribulation. It has shaped American evangelicalism and its popular fiction more than any other view, and its defenders prize its insistence that God's promises to Israel still stand. Each view has had faithful defenders, and Baptists have held all of them. This is third-order. It should never divide a church's table, because what every view confesses, the return, the resurrection and the judgment, is first-order.

sessions.title: The judgment
teaching: Many people hear the word judgment as the worst news in the Bible. For much of Scripture it is the best. The psalmists long for the day the Lord comes to judge the earth, because the oppressed have waited a long time for someone to set things right. Abraham, pleading for Sodom, staked everything on God's character: “Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?” (Genesis 18:25). A world without a final judgment is a world where the tyrant and his victim end the same way, and every wrong no court ever heard is simply forgotten. Miroslav Volf, a Croatian theologian writing out of the wars in the former Yugoslavia, argued that trust in God's judgment is what frees people to give up their own vengeance.

Scripture says the judge will be Christ, and that “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive his due for the things done in the body, whether good or bad” (2 Corinthians 5:10). How does judgment by works fit with justification by faith? Most traditions answer that works are evidence, not payment: the judgment brings into the open whether faith was real, and for those in Christ the verdict has already been spoken. Believers' works are also weighed for reward, and Catholic teaching has its own account of merit, itself grounded in grace. The judge was judged in our place. Those who trust him stand before a judge who has already borne the sentence.

sessions.title: Hell
teaching: No doctrine is harder to speak of, and none needs more honesty. Most of what the New Testament says about hell comes from Jesus himself, in images of fire, outer darkness and the destruction of body and soul that don't fit neatly together. What they share is loss: exclusion from the life of God for which people were made. Christians have read these words in three main ways. The view held by most of the church through its history, Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed and most evangelical, is eternal conscious punishment: the lost exist forever under God's just judgment. Its defenders point to Matthew 25:46, where eternal punishment and eternal life stand in one sentence, and agree with Augustine that one cannot end if the other does not.

Conditional immortality holds that only God is immortal in himself, that eternal life is his gift, and that the lost, after a just punishment, finally perish; its defenders note that Scripture's commonest words for their fate are death and destruction, and John Stott leaned tentatively toward it. Universal restoration, held by a few early voices such as Gregory of Nyssa and by some modern theologians, hopes that God's love will finally win every creature through judgment, reading the texts in which God reconciles all things. Most confessions reject universalism as a certainty, while many evangelicals count conditional immortality a minority view they can live beside. Whatever you conclude, hell should never be spoken of with relish, or without grief.

sessions.title: Heaven and the new creation
teaching: Many Christians picture the end as souls in a white, cloudy elsewhere, and some of the songs they sing encourage it. Scripture's last chapters picture something more solid. John sees a new heaven and a new earth, and a city coming down, and hears a voice from the throne: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them” (Revelation 21:3). The direction is downward. God does not finally take his people away from the world he made; he makes his home with them in it, renewed. Paul says that creation itself “will be set free from its bondage to decay” (Romans 8:21). What God called good in Genesis is not scrapped. It is healed.

Theologians have spoken of the heart of heaven in two ways that belong together. The older tradition, from Augustine through Thomas Aquinas, centers on the beatific vision, seeing God face to face, the joy to which every other joy was a sign. More recent writers, N. T. Wright among them in Surprised by Hope, have recovered the stress on a renewed earth, bodily life, and culture and work made whole. Both are biblical. John says “we will see Him as He is” (1 John 3:2), and Isaiah sees wolves and lambs at peace and houses built and lived in. The new creation is not less than God, and it is not less than a world. It is God at home with his people, at last.

sessions.title: Hope, and how it shapes life now
teaching: Christian hope is not optimism. Optimism reads the trends and expects them to improve; hope rests on a promise and a person, whatever the trends do. Peter says God “has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3). The hope is living because the Lord it rests on is alive. Jürgen Moltmann, who came to faith as a prisoner of war after the Second World War, put hope at the center of his Theology of Hope in 1964, arguing that the doctrine of the last things is not an appendix to Christian belief but the key to the whole of it. Many who disagree with him elsewhere still owe him that recovery.

Hope reshapes ordinary life. Paul ends his long chapter on the resurrection not with a vision but with an instruction: “Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58). If the body will be raised, caring for bodies matters. If creation will be renewed, faithful work is not wasted. If the Judge will set things right, you are free to forgive and to wait. Hope also makes room for lament, because only people who expect a better world can protest this one. Hope does not deny the dark. It refuses to call it final.

sessions.title: Speaking of hope to someone who is grieving
teaching: The doctrine of the last things is finally tested at a graveside, and the first thing to learn there is restraint. Grieving people have been hurt by Christians who explained too much, too soon: that God needed another angel, that everything happens for a reason, that the one who died would not want them to cry. None of that is the Christian hope. At the tomb of Lazarus, Jesus, who knew what he was about to do, still wept. Before he said anything to Martha about resurrection, he came. Presence comes before explanation. Often the most faithful thing to say is very little, and the most faithful thing to do is stay.

When words are wanted, the hope is simple enough to say plainly. Death is real, it is an enemy, and grief is the right response to it. Paul did not tell grieving Christians to stop grieving, but not to “grieve like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Jesus said to a woman whose brother had been four days in the grave, “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). Don't promise what Scripture doesn't, and don't hurry anyone. The hope is not that grief will end soon. It is that death does not have the last word, and neither does the grave you are standing beside.

sessions.question: Think of someone you know who is grieving: what would it look like to be present with them before you try to explain anything?
sessions.do: Read John 11:17-44 slowly. Write down what Jesus does before he speaks of resurrection, then write a two-sentence note of hope you could actually send to a grieving friend.

verse.text: Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies. And everyone who lives and believes in Me will never die. Do you believe this?”

care: If you are grieving someone who has died, these verses do not ask you to stop grieving. Jesus wept at his friend's grave (John 11:35). Paul says believers grieve, but not “like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, or you feel you do not want to go on, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. You do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is the most helpful thing anyone did for you, or said to you, when you were grieving?
discuss: What have Christians said to grieving people that hurt rather than helped, and why did it hurt?
In two or three sentences, how would you explain the Christian hope to a friend at a funeral, if they asked you?
Why does Jesus weep at Lazarus's tomb when he knows he is about to raise him, and what does that permit us?
group.pray: Pray for those who are grieving now, by name if you can, and ask for the grace to be present before you speak.
